question: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.

raiseTranscript.text: Our team assumed every support ticket needed a full manual review before routing. I pulled two weeks of ticket data and saw 40% were simple password resets that could be auto-routed. I built a quick rule in the ticketing system and tested it on a small queue.
Resolution time for those tickets dropped from 4 hours to 15 minutes. My manager had me roll it out to the whole team after I documented the edge cases.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Junior candidate analyzed ticket data, spotted 40% password resets, created auto-route rule
Tested on small queue then documented edge cases for full rollout
Outcome: 4h to 15min resolution
Quote: "I pulled two weeks of ticket data and saw 40% were simple password resets"
Follow-up: Asked what happened after test; candidate described manager review and rollout
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate identified a local process inefficiency by looking at their own queue data rather than waiting for direction. They tested the change at small scale before asking for broader rollout, which shows ownership of their work and coachability. The concrete before-and-after metric (4 hours to 15 minutes) is credible at this level. Biggest strength is the willingness to question an assumption and measure the result instead of just executing the existing process.

lowerTranscript.text: I noticed the team always did weekly status reports in a long email. I suggested we switch to a shared doc but my manager said it was fine the way it was so I dropped it.
Did you try anything else to test the idea?
No, I just moved on to my assigned tickets.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Candidate noticed weekly status email but stopped after one suggestion was rejected
No data, no small test, no follow-up attempt
Quote: "my manager said it was fine the way it was so I dropped it"
Follow-up: Asked if they tried anything else; candidate said they moved on to assigned work
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate identified a possible inefficiency but did not attempt any analysis or small experiment before accepting the first rejection. At this level we expect ownership of one's own work and at least one follow-up action when an idea is questioned. The story ends with the candidate reverting to assigned tasks rather than learning from the feedback. Biggest gap is lack of persistence or data to support the suggestion.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were duplicating API calls because each assumed their latency requirements were unique. I pulled cross-team metrics showing 70% overlap and ran a joint experiment to share one endpoint.
How did you get the other team to agree?
I showed them their own p99 numbers and let their on-call engineer run the test. Latency stayed flat and we cut 22k extra calls per day.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Senior candidate spotted duplicate API work across teams using shared metrics
Ran joint experiment after showing other team's own data
Outcome: 22k fewer calls/day with no latency regression
Quote: "I pulled cross-team metrics showing 70% overlap"
Follow-up: Asked how they got buy-in; candidate described letting the other on-call run the test
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate used cross-team data to surface an assumption that two teams were making independently and drove a joint experiment without formal authority. They let the other team validate the result themselves, which demonstrates influence through evidence rather than persuasion. The outcome is measurable and directly tied to the changed assumption. Biggest strength is the ability to create leverage across teams by sharing their own metrics instead of dictating a solution.

lowerTranscript.text: I thought our deployment process was too slow so I wrote a script to automate one step. The other team that owns the pipeline said no so I kept using the manual process.
Did you share any data with them?
I mentioned it in a meeting but didn't follow up.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Candidate automated one deployment step locally but stopped when owning team declined
No metrics shared, no experiment proposed
Quote: "the other team that owns the pipeline said no so I kept using the manual process"
Follow-up: Asked if data was shared; candidate said they mentioned it once
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate attempted a local improvement but did not produce cross-team data or propose a controlled test when the owning team pushed back. At senior level we expect evidence of influence without authority and clearer metrics. The story shows the candidate reverting to the status quo instead of iterating. Biggest gap is treating the rejection as final rather than using data to reopen the conversation.

raiseTranscript.text: My team assumed every feature needed a dedicated PM. After reviewing three launches I saw the PM was mostly translating between eng and design. I proposed rotating a designer into the role for two quarters and measured cycle time and decision quality.
How did the team react to the change?
Two engineers initially worried about missing product context. After the first retro they said decisions were faster because the designer was already in the room.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Manager questioned dedicated PM assumption after reviewing three launches
Tested designer rotation for two quarters with cycle-time and decision-quality metrics
Team feedback shifted from worry to faster decisions
Quote: "I proposed rotating a designer into the role for two quarters"
Follow-up: Asked about team reaction; candidate described initial concern then positive retro
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate used launch review data to question a structural assumption about role allocation and ran a time-boxed experiment that let the team experience the change. They tracked both quantitative metrics and qualitative team reaction, showing they own team outcomes rather than heroics. The story demonstrates developing the team by giving them direct exposure to product decisions. Biggest strength is creating leverage through role experimentation instead of adding headcount.

lowerTranscript.text: I decided the team should stop writing design docs because they took too long. I announced the change in a team meeting and told everyone to just start coding.
I had seen a couple of docs that were outdated so I made the call.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Manager unilaterally removed design docs based on a few outdated examples
No experiment, no metrics, no team input before announcement
Quote: "I announced the change in a team meeting and told everyone to just start coding"
Follow-up: Asked what data was used; candidate cited a couple of outdated docs
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate made a structural process change without data or team involvement and presented it as a directive. At manager level we look for how someone develops the team and creates leverage rather than issuing top-down decisions. The story lacks any measurement of the impact on decision quality or rework. Biggest gap is absence of experimentation or ownership of team outcomes.

raiseTranscript.text: We assumed every new market needed a local data center for latency. After modeling traffic patterns and customer growth I proposed a regional hub strategy instead. We ran a six-month pilot in one region and compared customer acquisition cost and infra spend.
The pilot showed we could support three new markets with 40% lower capex. We updated the three-year infrastructure plan and avoided two full data center builds.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Exec questioned local data center assumption using traffic and growth modeling
Six-month regional hub pilot with CAC and infra metrics
Result: 40% lower capex and revised three-year plan
Quote: "We ran a six-month pilot in one region and compared customer acquisition cost and infra spend"
Follow-up: Asked about longer-term effect; candidate described avoided builds and updated plan
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate surfaced a foundational infrastructure assumption and replaced it with a regional model after a controlled pilot that tied directly to business metrics. They translated the result into a multi-year capital plan change, showing strategic judgment and long-term thinking. The decision avoided significant future spend based on evidence rather than heroics. Biggest strength is using a limited experiment to shift org-level assumptions and resource allocation.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the board we should stop opening new data centers because cloud was cheaper. They asked for a plan and I said we would figure it out after the decision.
We had some high-level cloud pricing slides from a vendor.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you challenged an existing assumption or process and improved the outcome.
Exec recommended stopping data center builds based on vendor slides
No internal modeling or pilot before board discussion
Quote: "They asked for a plan and I said we would figure it out after the decision"
Follow-up: Asked what analysis supported it; candidate cited vendor pricing slides
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate challenged a major capital assumption without internal data or a phased approach, expecting the organization to commit before validating the trade-offs. At exec level we expect strategic judgment under ambiguity and the ability to de-risk large decisions. The story shows reliance on external slides rather than owned analysis. Biggest gap is lack of a measurable pilot or long-term plan before seeking approval.

diagnostic.junior: Documented edge cases for manager review
diagnostic.senior: Let other on-call run the test
diagnostic.exec: Pilot results fed into three-year plan
